In this exercise you'll write a working Arduino program from scratch, use the Serial Monitor to print output, and read from the built-in IMU sensor.

// Blink + Serial output void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT); Serial.println("Arduino Q — ready!"); } void loop() { digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, HIGH); Serial.println("LED ON"); delay(500); digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LOW); Serial.println("LED OFF"); delay(500); } To run it: Paste the code into a new sketch (File → New Sketch) Click Upload (→) Open Tools → Serial Monitor and set baud rate to 115200 You should see LED ON / LED OFF alternating

The Arduino Q has a built-in IMU. Let's read accelerometer values. #include <Arduino_LSM9DS1.h> void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); while (!Serial); if (!IMU.begin()) { Serial.println("IMU initialization failed!"); while (1); } Serial.println("IMU ready"); } void loop() { float x, y, z; if (IMU.accelerationAvailable()) { IMU.readAcceleration(x, y, z); Serial.print("X: "); Serial.print(x); Serial.print(" Y: "); Serial.print(y); Serial.print(" Z: "); Serial.println(z); } delay(100); } What to expect: Lay the board flat: Z ≈ 1.0, X ≈ 0, Y ≈ 0 Tilt it: watch X and Y change These raw acceleration values are what a gesture recognition model will learn from

If your board has an RGB LED (check your board pinout): // Adjust pin numbers for your specific board #define PIN_R 22 #define PIN_G 23 #define PIN_B 24 void setup() { pinMode(PIN_R, OUTPUT); pinMode(PIN_G, OUTPUT); pinMode(PIN_B, OUTPUT); } void setColor(int r, int g, int b) { analogWrite(PIN_R, r); analogWrite(PIN_G, g); analogWrite(PIN_B, b); } void loop() { setColor(255, 0, 0); delay(500); // Red setColor(0, 255, 0); delay(500); // Green setColor(0, 0, 255); delay(500); // Blue setColor(255, 165, 0); delay(500); // Orange setColor(128, 0, 128); delay(500); // Purple } tip Check your specific Arduino Q pinout diagram for the correct RGB LED pin numbers. These vary by board variant.
Before moving on, verify you can: Upload a sketch to the Arduino Q See Serial Monitor output Read IMU values that change when you move the board Control the LED

Get your development environment ready in four steps.

Download Arduino IDE 2.x from the official site: 👉 https://www.arduino.cc/en/software Choose your OS (Windows / macOS / Linux) and follow the installer. :::tip macOS On macOS, drag the Arduino IDE app to your Applications folder and open it once — macOS will ask to allow it. :::

Open Arduino IDE Go to File → Preferences (macOS: Arduino IDE → Settings) In the Additional boards manager URLs field, paste the URL for your Arduino Q package: https://downloads.arduino.cc/packages/package_index.json Click OK Go to Tools → Board → Boards Manager Search for your board (e.g., Arduino Mbed OS Nano Boards or Arduino Q) Click Install and wait for the download to complete

Plug your Arduino Q into your laptop using the USB-C cable from your kit Wait a few seconds for the OS to detect it Go to Tools → Port and select the port that appears (e.g., COM3 on Windows, /dev/cu.usbmodem... on macOS) Go to Tools → Board and select Arduino Q (or the matching board name) :::note Windows Users If no port appears, you may need to install the USB driver manually. Download it from the manufacturer's support page and run the installer, then reconnect the board. :::

Open Tools → Manage Libraries and install: Library Purpose Arduino_LSM9DS1 IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope) PDM Microphone (usually pre-installed) TensorFlowLite ML inference runtime ArduinoBLE Bluetooth LE (if needed) Search for each library by name and click Install.

Once everything is installed: Go to File → Examples → 01.Basics → Blink Click the Upload button (➡ arrow icon) Watch the built-in LED on your Arduino Q blink on and off If the LED blinks — you're all set! :::warning Upload Error? If you get an error like avrdude: stk500_getsync(), try: Double-pressing the reset button on the board to enter bootloader mode Re-selecting the port in Tools → Port Trying a different USB cable :::

This page covers the three core concepts of the workshop — what they are, how they connect, and what you need to know before the hands-on sessions.
Edge AI means running AI inference locally on a device — at the "edge" of the network — instead of sending data to a cloud server.
Cloud AI Edge AI Where it runs Remote server On the device Latency 100 ms – seconds < 10 ms Internet required Yes No Privacy Data leaves device Data stays on device Power High Milliwatts

Real-time response — a model on a microcontroller reacts in milliseconds Works offline — no Wi-Fi needed in the field Privacy-first — raw sensor data never leaves the device Low power — run for months on a coin cell

Data Collection → Feature Engineering → Training → Quantization ↓ Export (.tflite) → Deploy to Device → Inference Training happens on your laptop or in the cloud. Inference (the prediction step) runs on the Arduino Q itself.
Physical AI is AI that perceives and acts in the physical world — using sensors to read the environment and actuators to respond.
SENSORS ──▶ AI INFERENCE ──▶ ACTUATORS ▲ │ └────────── Feedback ──────────┘

Sensor What it measures Use case IMU (built-in) Acceleration + rotation Gesture recognition Microphone (built-in) Audio Keyword spotting DHT22 Temperature + humidity Environmental monitoring HC-SR04 Distance Object detection Reading the IMU: #include <Arduino_LSM9DS1.h> float ax, ay, az; IMU.readAcceleration(ax, ay, az); // ax/ay/az are in g (1.0 = 9.8 m/s²)

Actuator What it does Use case LED / RGB LED Light output Visual feedback SG90 Servo Rotates 0–180° Gesture control Active Buzzer Tone output Audio alerts Relay Switches mains loads Smart switch Controlling a servo: #include <Servo.h> Servo myServo; myServo.attach(9); myServo.write(90); // Rotate to 90°
Combining multiple sensors gives richer data: IMU + Microphone → gesture + voice recognition Temp + Humidity + CO₂ → air quality classification
TinyML is machine learning on microcontrollers — hardware that costs a few dollars and uses milliwatts of power.
Standard ML TinyML Hardware GPU server Microcontroller RAM GBs Kilobytes Power Hundreds of watts Microwatts–milliwatts Cost $thousands $1–$10

Keyword spotting — detect spoken words ("yes", "no", "go") from microphone audio. Gesture recognition — classify hand movements from IMU data. Anomaly detection — flag unusual sensor readings (predictive maintenance). Image classification — detect people or objects with a small camera.

A trained model uses 32-bit floats — too large for a microcontroller. Quantization converts weights to 8-bit integers: Format Size Speed Accuracy Float32 4× base Baseline Highest Int8 1× base 2–4× faster ~97–99% of Float32

The inference runtime that runs on your Arduino Q: // Simplified TFLM inference loop tflite::MicroInterpreter interpreter(model, resolver, tensor_arena, arena_size); interpreter.AllocateTensors(); // Feed sensor data as input float* input = interpreter.input(0)->data.f; input[0] = accel_x; input[1] = accel_y; input[2] = accel_z; // Run the model interpreter.Invoke(); // Read the prediction float* output = interpreter.output(0)->data.f; // output[i] = probability for class i

Edge Impulse handles the full pipeline in the browser — no ML expertise required: Collect sensor data from your Arduino Q Process — auto-extract features (FFT, MFCCs, spectrograms) Train — pick a model architecture, click Start Training Deploy — download an Arduino library, upload with one click

Physical World │ Sensors (IMU, Mic, DHT22…) ← Physical AI: perceive │ Signal Processing (windowing, FFT) ← TinyML: prepare features │ ML Inference (TFLM on Arduino Q) ← Edge AI: predict on-device │ Actuators (LED, Servo, Buzzer…) ← Physical AI: act Every project in this workshop follows this exact flow. Once you understand it, the rest is just filling in the details.

Edge AI means running artificial intelligence algorithms locally on a device — at the "edge" of the network — rather than sending data to a remote server or the cloud.

Cloud AI Edge AI Where it runs Remote server On the device itself Latency 100 ms – several seconds < 10 ms (real-time) Internet Required Not required Privacy Data leaves the device Data stays on device Power High (server) Ultra-low (mW range) Cost Per-API-call billing One-time hardware
A keyword-spotting model on a microcontroller responds in milliseconds. Sending audio to a cloud API and waiting for a response takes seconds — unacceptable for many applications.
Medical wearables, security cameras, and industrial sensors often can't (or shouldn't) send raw data over the internet. Edge AI keeps sensitive data local.
Edge devices function in remote locations, underground, or in poor-connectivity environments — no internet required.
A TinyML model on a microcontroller can run for months on a coin cell battery. Cloud-dependent systems require continuous data transmission.

Smart speakers — wake-word detection runs on-device; only triggered audio goes to the cloud Industrial predictive maintenance — vibration anomaly detection on factory floors Healthcare wearables — ECG classification, fall detection Agriculture — soil sensor analysis, pest detection with cameras Consumer electronics — face unlock, gesture control, noise cancellation Robotics — real-time object detection and navigation

Physical AI Systems Bootcamp is a hands-on, intensive program designed to equip students with practical skills in building intelligent embedded and robotic systems that operate at the edge — combining AI, sensors, and real-world actuation into deployable physical systems. This bootcamp bridges: Embedded Systems Edge Computing TinyML Intelligent Control Systems Robotics

By the end of the 2-day bootcamp, participants will be able to: Explain the difference between Cloud AI and Edge AI Understand the fundamentals of embedded systems using Arduino Q Implement a complete TinyML pipeline using Edge Impulse Deploy a trained model onto an Arduino Q Design a Physical AI system architecture (Sensor → Model → Decision → Actuator) Build and present a working intelligent embedded or robotic system Document technical work professionally
CS, ECE, EEE, IT — B.Tech / M.Tech / MCA / M.Sc students Mixed coding and Arduino experience (2nd, 3rd, 4th year) Maximum 20 students per batch Individual learning, group-based final project
Duration 2 Days Time 9:00 AM – 4:00 PM Includes Lunch break and short bio breaks

All projects follow the Physical AI system architecture: Sensor → Model → Decision → Actuator Day 1 ends with a guided project (done together as a group). Day 2 is your team's own build — pick one of the ideas below or propose your own.

The facilitator leads the full group through one complete Physical AI project from start to finish — data collection, model training on Edge Impulse, deployment to Arduino Q, and actuator response. This is your reference for Day 2. Project TBD based on batch — confirmed on Day 1.

Sensors: IMU (Accelerometer + Gyro) Model: Motion classification — TinyML on Edge Impulse Actuator: LED, Servo, Buzzer Idea: Classify specific hand gestures or arm movements and trigger a corresponding response (rotate servo, change LED colour, sound alert).

Sensors: USB Camera Model: Image classification — Edge Impulse FOMO or MobileNet Actuator: LED, Relay, Buzzer Idea: Detect a specific object, person presence, or condition from camera feed and trigger an action.

Sensors: USB Camera with built-in mic, or Microphone Module (if camera unavailable) Model: Sound classification — keyword spotting or event detection Actuator: LED, Servo, Buzzer Idea: Detect a specific sound (clap, voice command, alarm) and respond with an actuator.

Sensors: Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04), IMU Model: Obstacle detection / behaviour classification Actuator: 2WD Robot Chassis, DC Motors, Motor Driver Idea: A robot that navigates a path using distance sensing and an AI decision layer.

Sensors: USB Camera Model: Eye-state or head-pose classification Actuator: Buzzer alert Idea: Detect when a driver's eyes are closed or head is drooping and trigger an alert. (Autonomous Car Monitoring — driver sleeping use case.)

Sensors: USB Camera Model: Face detection / presence classification Actuator: OLED display, LED indicator Idea: Detect presence of a person and log attendance automatically using an on-device vision model.

Sensors: Temperature Sensor, Vibration Sensor Model: Anomaly detection autoencoder — Edge Impulse Actuator: Buzzer, LED alert Idea: Learn what "normal" looks like and flag deviations — mimics industrial predictive maintenance.
